analysis.one_liner: Rewrites federal labor law so misclassified independent contractors can unionize and bargain collectively.
analysis.headline: The bill was never given a hearing or a vote: after being referred to the Senate labor committee in November 2017, it sat untouched until the 115th Congress ended, so the only senators on record are the 1 sponsor and 8 cosponsors who introduced it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the National Labor Relations Act so that a worker counts as an employee, not an independent contractor, unless the company can show three things: the worker is truly free from the company's control, the work is outside the company's normal business, and the worker runs an independent business of their own. It would also tighten who counts as a supervisor, so only workers who spend most of their time supervising lose collective bargaining rights. The purpose is to stop companies from labeling workers as contractors to deny them the legal right to organize a union.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are currently treated as independent contractors while working under a company's direction—such as many ride-hailing and delivery drivers, franchise workers, and contract workers in trucking, janitorial, and home care—would gain the right to form unions and bargain over pay and working conditions. Their co-workers who win genuine bargaining would also gain a stronger floor for wages and benefits in the workplaces where organizing succeeds.

how_it_helps.text: Adopts a three-part test ('free from control, outside the usual course of the employer's business, independently established') under which any worker performing services is presumed an employee with collective bargaining rights, closing the main route companies use to strip workers of organizing rights [S2] [S3].

Narrows the definition of 'supervisor' so a worker only loses bargaining rights if they spend a majority of their work time exercising supervisory authority, and removes 'assign' and 'responsibly to direct' from the supervisor test [S3].
The stated aim of the bill is to prevent the misclassification of employees as independent contractors in order to deny them collective bargaining rights [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies whose business models depend on classifying workers as independent contractors—ride-hailing and delivery platforms, franchisors, staffing and temp agencies, and contract firms in trucking, janitorial, and home care—would bear higher labor costs, potential collective bargaining obligations, and legal exposure under the new test. Some workers who currently prefer contractor flexibility, and genuinely independent professionals, could see their status re-examined.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gig platforms, franchisors, and contractor-dependent firms

drawbacks.text: The three-part test could sweep in workers who function like genuinely independent businesses—consultants, freelancers, owner-operators who hire their own help—forcing companies to reclassify or restructure those relationships, with real costs for workers who value contractor flexibility [S3].

Reclassifying large numbers of contractors as employees would raise labor costs for platforms and contractor-dependent firms, which could mean fewer contracting opportunities, higher prices, or changes to how gig work is scheduled and assigned—costs an honest supporter would have to weigh [S2].

Narrowing the supervisor definition expands the set of workers covered by collective bargaining rules, a change employers would contest as intruding on management's ability to direct day-to-day work [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and large for a specific group: workers who are employees in every practical sense but are labeled contractors, and who currently have no legal right to bargain. The costs are real but manageable in principle—the test's carve-outs preserve true independent businesses—and the bill's design follows the test already used in several state laws. The main honest objection is transition disruption in industries built on the contractor model, and the bill offered no gradual phase-in.

outcome.mechanism: It was read and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended, so it simply expired.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on November 2, 2017, with 8 original cosponsors—7 Democrats and 1 Independent [S1] [S3] [S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action—no hearing, no markup, no floor vote—is recorded for the bill through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that classify workers as independent contractors avoided the higher costs and bargaining obligations the bill would have imposed, without ever having to argue against it on the floor. Workers hoping for bargaining rights got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to change the National Labor Relations Act's employee and supervisor definitions and referred it to the HELP Committee.

for.role: Original cosponsors (Sens. Gillibrand, Durbin, Franken, Merkley, Murray, Baldwin, Booker)

for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; Independent caucus

against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, letting it die in committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 supporting senators were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled Senate never acted on it.

industries.industry: Ride-hailing and delivery platforms (the gig economy)
industries.note: Their business models rest on classifying drivers as independent contractors; the bill's test would presume those workers are employees with union and bargaining rights, raising the platforms' labor costs. Workers' gain in bargaining power is the platforms' cost.

industries.industry: Franchisors and contractor-dependent firms (trucking, janitorial, home care, staffing agencies)
industries.note: These industries use contractor or franchise structures to set pay and conditions without bargaining obligations; the bill would narrow the supervisor definition and reclassify many of their workers, exposing them to collective bargaining.

Millions of newly covered workers would become potential members and bargaining units; the bill expands the population unions could organize. Its gain runs alongside workers' gain in bargaining rights.
The test's three carve-outs would keep truly independent businesses outside employee status, but some freelancers near the line could face reclassification or loss of contracting arrangements.
